senses.def: the act of catching something
senses.comment: Though in Greek the term ἄγρα may be used to refer to the catching of a wide variety of objects, in the context of Luke 5:4 the reference is to fish, and one must make certain that the appropriate term in the receptor language is employed, depending, for example, whether one catches fish, animals, or people.

senses.def: (derivative of Αἴγυπτος ‘Egypt,’ 93.398) pertaining to Egypt
(derivative of Αἴγυπτος ‘Egypt,’ 93.398) a person who is a native of Egypt

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to fail to exercise self-control
to compel someone to act in a particular manner
senses.comment: In some instances ἀναγκάζω and δέω[c] may be rendered as ‘to cause it to be necessary for.’ In other instances a simple causative seems to be the closest equivalent. For example, the last clause of Galatians 2:14 may be expressed as ‘how can you make Gentiles live like Jews,’ and in Acts 20:22 one may translate ‘and now the Spirit makes me go to Jerusalem.’

senses.def: pertaining to not being able to defend oneself or to justify one’s actions
(derivative of ἄνθρωπος[a] ‘people,’ 9.1) pertaining to being a person
senses.comment: Many languages, however, lack an adjectival form equivalent to ‘human,’ and therefore one may speak of ‘human wisdom’ as being ‘wisdom that people have.’ At the same time, languages may actually lack an abstract term such as ‘wisdom,’ and therefore it may be necessary to translate ‘taught by human wisdom’ as ‘taught by those people who are wise.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: human hand) a human being as a means of accomplishing something

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: pertaining to an inland or higher area, presumably away from the shoreline
to remove a piece of clothing quickly and cast it aside
to cause a state to cease by force and with the implication of elimination

(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀπορφανίζω ‘to cause to be an orphan,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause someone to be spacially separated, with the implication of additional emotional deprivation
any cardinal number
senses.comment: It may be important to add a marginal note to Revelation 13:18 to indicate that the number 666 was actually derived from adding up the numerical values of the letters of a name.

senses.def: the sum or total of a numbered quantity
a state of incapacity to do or experience something
senses.comment: A literal rendering of this expression in 2 Corinthians 12:9 may not be meaningful, and in fact can be quite misleading. δύναμις is best interpreted as ‘God’s power’ and ἀσθένεια as the weakness which Paul experienced. Therefore, one may be able to translate as ‘my power is greatest when you are weak’ (see Today’s English Version).

senses.def: the state of being ill and thus incapacitated in some manner
senses.comment: It may be extremely difficult in some languages to speak of ‘taking illness’ or ‘carrying away diseases.’ A strictly literal rendering of such an expression might suggest immediately that Jesus was a type of medicine man who healed others by taking upon himself precisely the same kinds of diseases (a widespread shamanistic practice). It may therefore be necessary in some languages to translate Matthew 8:17 as ‘he caused us to no longer have illness and disease.’ In this way, one may avoid a specific type of shamanistic practice which would be inappropriate in this context.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀσθένεια[a] ‘weakness,’ 74.23) a state of timidity resulting from a lack of confidence
a walled enclosure either to enclose human activity or to protect livestock
senses.comment: A sheepfold may be described in some languages as ‘a place for sheep with a wall built around it’ or ‘a corral for sheep’ or ‘a place for protecting sheep.’

senses.def: an open area enclosed by structures within a building complex, such as the temple, a palace, or a house; or any dwelling having such an enclosed open area (often a relatively elaborate structure)
pertaining to a state of not having life
senses.comment: In some translations it may seem strange or even meaningless to speak of ‘musical instruments’ as being ‘lifeless’ or ‘not alive,’ since everyone would obviously know such a fact. It may therefore be necessary to translate as ‘even musical instruments like the flute and the harp, which are obviously not alive, nevertheless produce a sound.’

senses.def: the daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of Herod Agrippa II
to desire to have or experience something, with the implication of some reasoned planning or will to accomplish the goal

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: to think, with the purpose of planning or deciding on a course of action
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are two quite distinct sets of terms for planning depending upon the purpose involved in such planning. If the planning is constructive, either for oneself or someone else, one set of terms is likely to be used, while if the planning is harmful (usually against someone else), another set of terms would be used.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: people living at the same time and belonging to the same reproductive age-class
senses.comment: The expression ‘the people of this generation’ may also be expressed as ‘the people living now’ or ‘the people of this time.’ Successive generations may be spoken of as ‘groups of people who live one after the other’ or ‘successions of parents and children.’

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: an ethnic group exhibiting cultural similarities
senses.comment: Compare γενεά[a] those of the same time (11.4).

senses.def: successive following generations of those who are biologically related to a reference person
senses.comment: In the case of γενεά[c], τέκνον[b], and σπέρμα[b] (10.29), the reference is not to one’s immediate descendants or offspring (that is to say, to one’s sons or daughters) but to a successive series of such persons, one’s descendants. In some languages such descendants may be called merely ‘the children of one’s children,’ and in other languages one may refer to descendants as ‘those who follow one’ or ‘those who come later.’

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: an indefinite period of time, but in close relationship to human existence and in some contexts, a period of time about the length of a generation
senses.comment: It is, of course, possible in Acts 14:16 that the reference should be to ‘generations’ in the sense of periods of time.

senses.def: an adult female person of marriageable age
senses.comment: In some languages it may be awkward to speak of ‘arresting men and women,’ since it is normal in such languages to speak of ‘men and women’ simply as ‘people.’ However, where the distinction of ‘men and women’ can be employed, it should be done, since the arresting of women for presumed heresy in NT times would seem far less justified than the arresting of men, who were supposed to take a more active part in new movements and thus were more likely to be arraigned before authorities.|As a form of address, γυνή was used in Koine Greek in speaking politely to a female person: ὦ γύναι, μεγάλη σου ἡ πίστις ‘Lady, your faith is great’ Matthew 15:28. In John 2:4 Jesus uses γυνή to address his mother courteously.|In a number of languages it would be totally impossible to have Jesus address his mother merely as ‘woman.’ To do so in some languages would imply that Jesus was denying that Mary was his mother. In other languages, such an expression would imply that Jesus was calling his mother a prostitute or evil person. Accordingly, in a number of languages there is simply no other way in which Jesus could address his mother than as ‘mother’ or ‘my mother.’

senses.def: a woman who is married to a man
senses.comment: The distinctions in meaning of γυνή[a] woman (9.34) and γυνή[b] wife parallel those involving ἀνήρ[c] and ἄνθρωπος[c] (see 10.53). A number of languages, however, employ essentially the same usage as Greek in that a wife is simply called his woman, my woman, etc. The contexts normally indicate clearly which meaning of γυνή is involved.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to touch a woman) to marry a woman
senses.comment: It is important to note that this expression in the second part of 1 Corinthians 7:1 may be either a statement by Paul or a quotation from a letter from the church of Corinth. This fact should be clearly noted in the margin.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to take a woman) to marry a woman
(an idiom, literally: to have a woman) to be married to a woman
(derivative of δεσμός[b] ‘to be in prison,’ 37.115) a person who is under custody in prison
to cause a group or gathering to disperse or scatter, with possible emphasis on the distributive nature of the scattering (that is to say, each going in a different direction)
to cause someone to awaken

senses.subdomain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs
senses.def: a marker of a causative relation, with the implication of a significant change in state
to become awake after sleeping

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of διεγείρομαι[a] ‘to become awake from sleep,’ 23.74) to become rough, in reference to a surface of water
senses.comment: In describing a rough surface of a body of water, one may say in some languages ‘there were many waves’ or ‘the waves were very big.’ In other languages one may speak of a rough surface of a body of water by an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘the face of the water was foaming’ or ‘the water was angry.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of δολιόω ‘to deceive,’ 88.154) pertaining to using treachery in order to deceive
(derivative of Εβραῖος ‘a Hebrew,’ 93.105) pertaining to the Hebrews
senses.comment: The addition of γράμμασιν in some manuscripts literally applies to Hebrew letters, though the reference seems to be to the language, probably Aramaic. In Acts 21:40 a peculiar form of Ἑβραϊκός occurs, namely, Ἑβραΐδι. Scholars, however, explain it as from Ἑβραΐς, relating it to Εβραῖος (93.105).

senses.def: extension toward a special goal
extension toward a goal which is inside an area

senses.subdomain: On, Upon, On the Surface Of
senses.def: a position on the surface of an area
a position defined as being within certain limits
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects
a marker of intent, often with the implication of expected result
a marker of result, with the probable implication of a preceding process
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret εἰς in this construction of 2 Thessalonians 1:5 as purpose (see εἰς[f], 89.57).|It would be possible to interpret εἰς … ἄγω in Romans 2:4 as being purely an expression of cause since ἄγω[g] (see 36.1) also involves a component of cause, and therefore one may interpret the expression εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει as ‘it causes you to repent.’ In either case, however, εἰς marks a resulting event or state.

senses.def: a marker of the means by which one event makes another event possible
(with the accusative) a marker of content as a means of specifying a particular referent

senses.subdomain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
senses.def: a degree extending to a particular point as marked by the context
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 10:15 περισσείαν itself indicates a superabundant degree of something (see 78.31), while εἰς marks a degree up to such a point. One may say, therefore, that semantically εἰς serves to reinforce the meaning of περισσείαν.

senses.def: a marker of a change of state
a marker of an involved experiencer
senses.comment: It is possible to translate 1 Peter 1:11 as ‘trying to find out when the time would be and how it would come’ by interpreting εἰς in 1 Peter 1:11 as εἰς[i] (90.23) and ποῖον as ποῖος[b] (58.30).

senses.def: (with the accusative) a marker of persons benefited by an event, with the implication of something directed to them
senses.comment: In both 1 Corinthians 16:1 and 2 Corinthians 8:4 there is clearly an ellipsis of an event of ‘sending’ such help to and on behalf of God’s people.

senses.def: (with the dative) a marker of objects which serve as symbolic substitutes for supernatural persons or powers presumed to act as guarantors of compliance with oaths

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: a marker of an extent of time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of εἰς τέλος in 1 Thessalonians 2:16 (as an idiom), see 78.47.

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: a marker of a unit of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: the continuous extent of time up to a point
senses.comment: The phrase εἰ μὴ ὅταν is often translated as ‘until’ (for example, μηδενὶ ἅ εἶδον διηγήσωνται, εἰ μὴ ὅταν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ‘not to tell anybody what they have seen until the Son of Man has risen from death’ Mark 9:9), but this phrase may be analyzed as meaning ‘if it is not when,’ an expression which is semantically equivalent to ‘until.’|For an interpretation of εἰς τέλος in John 13:1 as an idiom, see 78.47.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to come into knowledge) to acquire information about something, with emphasis upon the process involved
senses.comment: It is also possible to treat the phrase εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἔρχομαι as meaning ‘to come to know’ in the sense of ‘to come to understand’ (see 32.17).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to come into knowledge) to come to understand the meaning of something, with special emphasis upon the process
senses.comment: One may also interpret εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἔρχομαι as meaning ‘to come to have knowledge of, to come to know’ (see 27.4).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: into that which is not measured) a point on a scale going beyond what is expected
senses.comment: In a number of languages one can perhaps best render this statement in 2 Corinthians 10:13 as ‘we will not boast too much’ or ‘we will boast only so much.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: unlimited duration of time, with particular focus upon the future
senses.comment: See also Luke 1:33; 2 Peter 3:18; Jude 1:25; Hebrews 1:8. The more elaborate expressions employing αἰών are somewhat more emphatic in meaning and are to be found especially in the solemn style of doxologies.|For another interpretation of εἰς τὸ παντελές in Hebrews 7:25, see 78.47.

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: into the ear) pertaining to what is known only by those who hear a particular message in private
senses.comment: A phrase such as ‘whatever you hear in secret’ may be rendered as ‘whatever you hear when no one else is listening.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to come to the worse) to become increasingly more sick

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be in the gall of bitterness) to be particularly envious or resentful of someone

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to show kindness or concern for someone in serious need
to carry on a business involving buying and selling
to demand that a person take an oath as to the truth of what is said or as to the certainty that one will carry out the request or command
glosses: to insist that one take an oath
senses.comment: It is extremely difficult to translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω in a literal manner, though in some contexts one can say ‘I put you under oath,’ but in a number of passages the person speaking is imploring and not necessarily in a position to command or insist. Therefore, in a passage such as Mark 5:7, one may render the meaning idiomatically as ‘for God’s sake, I ask you, do not punish me.’ In 1 Thessalonians 5:27 one may translate ‘in the name of the Lord, I ask you to read this letter to all the Christian brothers,’ and in Matthew 26:63 one may translate ‘in the name of the living God, I charge you, Tell us who you are.’|In most languages one may translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω by simply adding a causative component to terms meaning ‘to swear’ or ‘to take an oath.’ In other words, ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω may be rendered as ‘to cause a person to say under oath.’

senses.def: cause someone to be so astounded as to be practically overwhelmed
to be so astonished as to almost fail to comprehend what one has experienced
to think or reason in a completely irrational manner
glosses: to not be in one’s right mind
to be out of one’s mind

senses.subdomain: Beyond, On the Other Side Of
senses.def: a position farther away than a reference point

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: that which is intended or purposed as the result of thinking
to build or construct something on some specified location
to increase the potential of someone or something, with focus upon the process involved
one who announces the gospel
senses.comment: Though the term εὐαγγελιστής indicates only an individual who ‘announces the gospel,’ early usage would suggest that this was often a person who went from place to place announcing the good news.

senses.def: coarse jesting involving vulgar expressions and indecent content
to tuck up or hold a garment firmly in place by wrapping a belt, girdle, or piece of cloth around it
glosses: to wear a narrow band of cloth around the waist

senses.def: to dress oneself, including the fastening of one’s belt as the final act in dressing
a state of wonderment or amazement, usually with the implication of marveling
an event which causes someone to wonder or marvel

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: hair, either of a person or of an animal
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made between the hair of animals and the hair of humans. Further distinctions may also be made between the hair of the head, the hair of the beard, and general body hair. In certain instances special terms are also used for pubic hair.

senses.def: the state of being adequate or qualified for something
to insult in a particularly strong and unjustified manner
to judge someone as definitely guilty and thus subject to punishment
glosses: to render a verdict of guilt

senses.def: to make someone completely adequate or sufficient for something
glosses: to cause to be fully qualified

senses.def: heat sufficiently intense to cause suffering or burning
senses.comment: In some languages the effect of heat may be described simply as ‘heat will not scorch them’ or ‘they will not suffer because of heat’ (Revelation 7:16). Such expressions, however, may be ambiguous because they might mean that the individuals involved would be able to easily withstand the heat. The meaning of the biblical passage, however, is that there would be no heat to cause them harm.

senses.def: to weep or wail, with emphasis upon the noise accompanying the weeping
senses.comment: In Matthew 2:18 κλαίω occurs with a so-called ‘direct object,’ for example, Ραχὴλ κλαίουσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς … ὅτι οὐκ εἰσίν ‘Rachel weeps for her children … because they are all dead.’ The so-called direct object is, however, the cause of the weeping, and the so-called transitive usage of κλαίω does not alter the meaning.

senses.def: to wear long hair as part of one’s attire
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate κομάω as ‘to let one’s hair grow long’ or ‘not to cut one’s hair.’

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (locative derivative of κρυπτός ‘secret, hidden,’ 28.69) a place which is secret or hidden and thus not generally known, possibly referring to a structure built underground for hiding or storing objects
the state of brightness or shining
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between some object which is bright in and of itself (that is to say, the source of brightness or radiance) and objects which are bright because they reflect light from some source. In the case of Matthew 17:5 (which is generally regarded as a reference to the Shekinah presence of God), the cloud would not be merely reflecting light but would be a source of light (see 14.50).

senses.def: to think about something in a detailed and logical manner
to keep a mental record of events for the sake of some future action
senses.comment: ‘To keep a mental record of something’ may be rendered as ‘to add up in one’s mind’ or ‘to make a list in one’s heart.’

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
to keep records of commercial accounts, involving both debits and credits
a state of happiness, implying favorable circumstances
senses.comment: In Galatians 4:15 μακαρισμός clearly refers to a state of happiness which occurred in the past but which was no longer evident. It may therefore be necessary to indicate that the happiness in question is past, and accordingly, one may translate ‘you were so happy! What has happened?’ or ‘then you were so happy! What has happened to you now?’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to become drunk on alcoholic beverages

senses.subdomain: Appearance as an Outward Manifestation of Form
senses.def: to cause a change in the form of something
glosses: to change from one form into another

senses.def: to relate something to something else on the basis of certain correspondences
a construction for the burial of the dead; often a natural cave or hewn out of bedrock
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between a grave (a hole in the ground in which a corpse is placed) and a tomb (a construction built above the surface of the ground for housing a corpse). In some contexts, however, it may be better to use a more generic expression, for example, ‘places where people are buried’ or ‘places where corpses are placed.’ In Mark 5:2 it is important to avoid a term which would designate merely graves, for the demoniac who met Jesus was not living down in graves in the ground, but had found some habitation either in burial caves or in tombs constructed above ground.|It is also possible to translate μνημεῖα in Matthew 23:29 as ‘monuments to the dead’ (see 7.76).

senses.def: a monument built as a memorial to someone who has died
senses.comment: Constructions such as those mentioned in Luke 11:47 could also serve as tombs for the individuals in question. For a discussion of μνημεῖον in Matthew 23:29, see 7.75.

senses.def: a building in which a deity is worshiped (in the case of the Temple in Jerusalem, a place where God was also regarded as dwelling)
senses.comment: ναός[a] may often be rendered as ‘the house of God’ or ‘the place where God dwells’ or ‘God’s building.’ In some languages it is most naturally referred to as ‘the holy house’ or ‘the holy place.’ See also 7.16.|ναός is used figuratively in John 2:21 (ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔλεγεν περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ ‘but he spoke of the temple of his body’ or ‘… of his body as a temple’) and in 1 Corinthians 6:19, where the believer’s body is spoken of as ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματος ‘the temple of the Holy Spirit within you.’

senses.def: a small replica or model of a temple or shrine
senses.comment: In Acts 19:24 the term ναός refers only to a small replica of the temple of Artemis. An equivalent of ναός[b] in Acts 19:24 is in some languages ‘tiny temples of Artemis,’ or, in other instances, it is ‘souvenir temples of Artemis.’

senses.def: (derivative of νομοθετέω ‘to give a law,’ 33.339) one who gives or enacts laws
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not possible to speak literally of a ‘lawgiver’ as ‘one who gives laws,’ for laws seem to be quite distinct from gifts. However, the same meaning is often communicated by somewhat different expressions, for example, ‘one who decides what people must do’ or ‘one who makes a law stand’ or ‘one who gives strength to a law.’

senses.def: (derivative of οἰκέω[a] ‘to dwell,’ 85.67) a place in which one may dwell
a marker of association, based on similarity of activity or state
patterned rhythmic movements of the whole and/or parts of the body, normally to the accompaniment of music
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are highly specific terms for various types of dancing, and one must make certain that the appropriate expression is used. Some terms for dancing may refer only to erotic dances; others, to highly ritualized performances in drama or religious practice; and still others may refer to personal expressions of happiness, joy, or grief. Special care must be exercised in selecting a term which will fit the context.

senses.def: pertaining to being subject to suffering
to be present at a particular time and place
to allow not to do
to suffer weakness or disability in some part of the body
senses.comment: In some languages ‘weak hands’ may be expressed as ‘hands that cannot hold anything’ or ‘hands that cannot do anything.’

senses.def: pertaining to the lack of the essential means of livelihood
to cut off the foreskin of the male genital organ as a religious rite involving consecration and ethnic identification
senses.comment: In the case of societies which practice circumcision, there is normally a perfectly satisfactory term to designate this type of operation, though it may not have any religious significance but only be a part of puberty ritual. For societies which do not practice circumcision or are not well acquainted with such a practice, a term which specifically describes the operation may be both offensive and vulgar. It may therefore be necessary to use a borrowing or to employ a somewhat obscure term such as ‘to cut around’ and then to explain the specific meaning of the term or phrase in a glossary.|Even in the case of societies which practice circumcision, there may be problems in comprehension of the significance of such an act, and these difficulties may require marginal notes. If, for example, a society practices circumcision only in connection with puberty rites, it may seem inexplicable that Jesus would have been circumcised on the eighth day after his birth (Luke 2:21). In many societies such an act would seem to be either a deed of extreme cruelty to a baby or a sign of mature sexuality in an infant.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (a set phrase, literally: those of circumcision) those who insisted on circumcising Gentiles if they were to be regarded as true believers in Jesus Christ
glosses: those of the circumcision or those who insisted on circumcision

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: either side of the trunk of the body
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to the side of the body, since terms differ depending on whether the area involves (1) the ribs, (2) the area between the ribs and the pelvic bone, or (3) the area of the hip, from the fleshy mid-part of the trunk to the leg.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being morally corrupt and evil
senses.comment: In translating Matthew 5:11 it is important to indicate that the words spoken are not evil in themselves, but the content of what is spoken involves attributing evil and wicked deeds to the followers of Jesus. It may, therefore, be necessary to say in some languages ‘when men speak against you by saying that you have done wicked deeds.’

senses.def: pertaining to possessing a serious fault and consequently being worthless
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must speak of ‘bad fruit’ in the context of Matthew 7:18 as ‘fruit which does not taste good.’ It is often wrong to use an expression such as ‘rotten fruit,’ since a good tree may produce fruit which rots as a result of being overly ripe.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to guilt resulting from an evil deed
senses.comment: In a number of languages it would be entirely misleading to speak of ‘a guilty conscience,’ for this would seem to imply that there is something sinful about the conscience itself. In reality, it is the conscience that says that a person is guilty, and therefore it may be necessary to translate Hebrews 10:22 as ‘with hearts that have been purified from a condition in which their conscience has said that they are guilty.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πονηρός[a] ‘evil,’ 88.110) a state of being sickly or diseased (in the NT with special reference to the eyes)
senses.comment: For other interpretations of πονηρός with ὀφθαλμός, see 57.108 and 88.165. See also 23.132.

senses.def: (a title for the Devil, literally: the evil one) the one who is essentially evil or in a sense personifies evil

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: evil eye) a feeling of jealousy and resentment because of what someone else has or does
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός in Matthew 20:15 as meaning ‘stinginess’ (see 57.108). See also 23.149.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: evil eye) to be stingy
senses.comment: It is also possible that ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός in Matthew 20:15 is to be understood in the sense of ‘jealous’ (see 88.165). See also 23.149.

senses.def: to hear before or previously to an event in question
to move up to a point (with the possible implication of higher status)
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to translate this expression in Luke 14:10 as ‘come up to a higher place’ or ‘come up to a better seat’ or ‘come up to a more important place.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to make unjust distinctions between people by treating one person better than another
senses.comment: ‘To show favoritism’ or ‘to be partial’ is expressed in an idiomatic manner in some languages, for example, ‘to look only upon a person’s face,’ ‘to call a sparrow a chicken,’ or ‘to give one’s clansman the best piece of meat.’

senses.def: to be sick with a fever
senses.comment: Though in a number of languages one can say ‘a person has a fever,’ in some languages the reverse expression is used, for example, ‘the fever has a person.’ Similarly, instead of saying ‘a person has a disease,’ it is ‘the disease which grabs a person.’ One may often speak of a fever as ‘to become hot’ or ‘to burn’ or ‘to be sick with burning.’

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: the movement of a liquid in some direction
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term referring to the flow of liquid may also be applied to the movement of any object, so that a literal rendering might be ‘the liquid moved.’ However, terms for ‘flow’ or ‘pour’ often differ substantially on the basis of the direction of the flow. For example, if the flow is relatively horizontal, and therefore slow, it may have one term, while if it is quite fast, another expression may be used, and if the flow is almost perpendicular (as in the case of pouring), a still different term is employed.

senses.def: (a set phrase, literally: flow of blood) the loss of blood through menstrual bleeding

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
senses.def: a pliable instrument of binding
glosses: chain (made of metal) or rope (made of fiber)
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term for chain is simply metal rope. In other languages it may be described as linked rope in contrast with twisted rope, that is, a rope made out of some kind of fiber.|The phrase σειραῖς ζόφου (2 Peter 2:4) is admittedly a strange expression, and in some manuscripts this gave rise to a slight change in orthography (σιροῖς; see 1.59) with the resulting meaning being ‘in pits of darkness.’ If, however, one adopts the text ἀλλὰ σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας, it may be possible to interpret the entire expression as ‘but he chained them in the darkness of hell.’

senses.def: to come to dwell in a place defined psychologically or spiritually (with the possible implication in some contexts of a temporary arrangement)
senses.comment: In all of these contexts, σκηνόω and ἐπισκηνόω are essentially figurative in meaning, for they deal with spiritual existence and residence rather than human residence or dwelling. In translating one should, in so far as possible, try to preserve this important figurative relationship, since it expresses one of the most significant ways in which spiritual and human existence can be combined. In some languages, however, it may be necessary to employ an expression which means simply ‘to be in’ or ‘to continue with,’ since expressions for ‘living’ or ‘dwelling’ may be based upon terms which are too specific in meaning, for example, ‘to eat from the same pot’ or ‘to enter by the same door.’

senses.def: the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
senses.comment: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, σπέρμα, σπόρος), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’|See also 10.23 for σπορά ‘seed’ used figuratively of descendants.

senses.def: small bird; speckled brown in color; genus Passer; roosts and nests in groups; eats grass seeds and grain; associated with the poor
senses.comment: The Greek term στρουθίον no doubt refers to the so-called ‘house sparrow,’ which almost always builds its nests near human habitation. In the Orient a similar type of sparrow exists, and a term designating such a sparrow can be used in all contexts in which the Greek term στρουθίον is employed.

senses.def: to share in something by having an appropriate part
glosses: to have a part of together with others

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a socio-political group acting as a judicial council
senses.comment: There are certain problems involved in the rendering of συνέδριον[a] as ‘city council,’ since in so many parts of the world a group which would be designated as a ‘city council’ would be primarily legislative rather than judicial in function. It is for that reason that συνέδριον[a] may be better translated in a number of instances as ‘the council which will judge you‘ or ‘before a group of men who will decide whether you have done right or wrong.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the highest Jewish council, exercising jurisdiction in civil and religious matters, but having no power over life and death or over military actions or taxation
senses.comment: In a number of languages συνέδριον[b] can be rendered by a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘the most important council of the Jews’ or ‘the council that made decisions for the Jewish people.’

senses.def: to crucify someone at the same time that another person is being crucified
the capital of Cilicia in southeast Asia Minor
the father of Bartimaeus
(an idiom, literally: to make straight wheel tracks for the feet) to live or behave in strict conformance to a predetermined model for behavior
a position above another, whether or not in contact

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a marker of superior status, suggesting an additional factor of degree
to spread out something underneath

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of ill will toward someone because of some real or presumed advantage experienced by such a person
senses.comment: Expressions for ‘envy’ or ‘jealousy’ are often idiomatic, for example, ‘the heart burns’ or ‘the stomach is hot.’

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: to cause someone to have misleading or erroneous views concerning the truth
(derivative of χαρίζομαι[a] ‘to give graciously and generously,’ 57.102) that which is given freely and generously
pertaining to the wearing of a gold ring
a somewhat more emphatic marker of similarity between events and states
